--- title: "Model Diagnostic" sidebar: start --- The BF class can compute model diagnostics for a given model. Lets consider the following model for a linear regression: $$ Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\alpha + \beta X_i, \sigma) $$ $$ \alpha \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) $$ $$ \beta \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) $$ $$ \sigma \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 50) $$ ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#d8963e92 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf import jax.numpy as jnp # setup platform------------------------------------------------ m = bf(platform="cpu") # import data ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path=True) m.data(data_path, sep=";") m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] m.scale(data=["weight"]) # define model ------------------------------------------------ def model(weight, height): a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name="a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name="b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name="s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs=height, shape=(weight.shape[0],)) # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, num_samples=500, num_chains=4) m.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` An NVIDIA GPU may be present on this machine, but a CUDA-enabled jaxlib is not installed. ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r library(BayesForge) # setup platform------------------------------------------------ m <- importBF(platform = "cpu") # import data ------------------------------------------------ data_path <- m$load$howell1(only_path = TRUE) m$data(data_path, sep = ";") m$df <- m$df[m$df$age > 18, ] m$scale(list("weight")) m$data_to_model(list("weight", "height")) # define model ------------------------------------------------ model <- function(weight, height) { a <- bf.dist.normal(178, 20, name = "a") b <- bf.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name = "b") s <- bf.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = "s") bf.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs = height, name = "height") } # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m$fit(model, num_samples = 500, num_chains = 4) m$summary() ``` ## Julia ```julia using PyBayesForge # setup platform------------------------------------------------ m = importBF(platform = "cpu") # import data ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path = true) m.data(data_path, sep = ";") m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] m.scale(["weight"]) # define model ------------------------------------------------ @BF function model(weight, height) a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name = "a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name = "b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = "s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs = height) end # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, num_samples = 500, num_chains = 4) m.summary() ``` ::: For additional documentation check the [diagnostics API reference](../reference/diag.qmd) Every plot takes `x_label=` and `y_label=` to replace the axis titles (`title=` for the plot title). A string sets the title of every panel; a list sets one per panel, in order (`None` keeps a panel's own title), for example `m.diag.posterior(x_label=["intercept", "slope", "sigma"])`. ## Predictions from model based on specific data value By default (`posterior=True`, `samples=None`), `m.sample(...)` evaluates the predictive distribution across all posterior MCMC draws (here $500 \times 4 = 2000$ draws). To obtain a single predicted value instead of the full posterior predictive vector, you can draw a single sample (`samples=1`), take the posterior predictive mean, or evaluate at fixed parameter values (`posterior=...`): ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#be5528a1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.sample() # Predictions from model based on data in data_on_model pred = m.sample(data=dict(weight=jnp.array([0.4])), remove_obs=False) # Full posterior predictive (2000 draws) # 1. Single random predictive draw from the posterior m.sample(data=dict(weight=jnp.array([0.4])), remove_obs=False, samples=1) # 2. Posterior predictive mean across all 2000 draws jnp.mean(pred["height"]) # 3. Single draw at fixed parameter values m.sample( data=dict(weight=jnp.array([0.4])), posterior=dict(a=154.6, b=5.8, s=5.1), remove_obs=False, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'height': Array([[149.99351347]], dtype=float64)} ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$sample() # Predictions from model based on data in data_on_model pred <- m$sample(data = list(weight = jnp$array(c(0.4))), remove_obs = FALSE) # Full posterior predictive (2000 draws) # 1. Single draw at fixed parameter values m$sample( data = list(weight = jnp$array(c(0.4))), posterior = list(a = 154.6, b = 5.8, s = 5.1), remove_obs = FALSE ) ``` ## Julia ```julia m.sample() # Predictions from model based on data in data_on_model pred = m.sample(data = pydict(weight = jnp.array([0.4])), remove_obs = false) # Full posterior predictive (2000 draws) # 1. Single random predictive draw from the posterior m.sample(data = pydict(weight = jnp.array([0.4])), remove_obs = false, samples = 1) # 2. ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$plot_ess() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.plot_ess() ``` ::: See [`m.diag.plot_ess`](../reference/diag.qmd#plot_ess) for further information regarding the list of arguments. ## Posterior predictive checks All posterior predictive checks compare the observed outcome with *predictions*: datasets of the outcome simulated by the fitted model, one per posterior draw (`m.diag.get_yrep()`). Both are taken from the fitted model automatically, and the plots are labelled with the name of the observed site (here `height`, from `obs=height`). With several observed sites, each function returns one figure per site; pass `site=` to choose one. The idea is always the same: if the model is good, the data it simulates should look like the real data. For count or categorical outcomes, [`m.diag.ppc_bars()`](../reference/diag.qmd#ppc_bars) and [`m.diag.ppc_rootogram()`](../reference/diag.qmd#ppc_rootogram) instead compare observed counts with predicted counts per category. **Which check for which model.** The model pages show the checks that matter for each kind of model: - Varying effects, one panel per group (`group=`): [Varying slopes](../16.%20Varying%20slopes.qmd), [Nested varying effects](../17.%20Nested%20varying%20effects.qmd), [Categorical variable](../4.%20Categorical%20variable.qmd). - A group effect the model leaves out: [Binomial model](../5.%20Binomial%20model.qmd) (one intercept for all chimpanzees). - Predictions along a covariate (`x=`, optionally with `group=`): [Interaction between continuous variables](../3.%20Interaction%20between%20continuous%20variables.qmd), [Poisson model with offset](../8.%20Poisson%20mode%20with%20offset.qmd), [Gaussian processes](../19.%20Gaussian%20processes.qmd). - Counts and over-dispersion (`ppc_rootogram`, `ppc_stat(stat="sd")`): [Gamma-Poisson](../9.%20Gamma-Poisson.qmd), [Beta binomial model](../6.%20Beta%20binomial%20model.qmd). - Excess of zeros (`ppc_stat(stat="n_zero")`): [Zero inflated](../13.%20Zero%20inflated.qmd). - Categorical outcomes (`ppc_bars`): [Categorical model](../10.%20Categorical%20model.qmd). ### Density overlay Overlays the density of the observed data (black) with the densities of n predicted datasets (blue). The black curve should look like one more blue curve; a different shape (two modes, skewness, mass below 0 for a positive outcome) points to a missing group or a wrong likelihood. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#eba19abd .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_density() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` /home/sosa/work/BF/BayesForge/Diagnostic/ppc.py:82: RuntimeWarning: ⚠️This function is still in development. Use it with caution. ⚠️ warn_dev("ppc") ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_density() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_density() ``` ::: See [`m.diag.ppc_density`](../reference/diag.qmd#ppc_density) for further information regarding the list of arguments. ### Test statistic Each predicted dataset is summarised by one number T (the curve is the distribution of T over the predictions) and T of the observed data is marked by the vertical line. The title gives the Bayesian p-value P(T(predicted) ≥ T(observed)) and its two-sided version: around 0.5 is fine, a two-sided value below 0.05 means the model does not reproduce this aspect of the data. Choose the statistic with `stat=`: `"mean"` (default), `"median"`, `"sd"`, `"var"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"q25"`, `"q75"`, `"skew"`, `"n_zero"`, `"n_pos"`, or (Python) any function of a 1D array, for example `stat=lambda v: np.percentile(v, 90)`. The mean is almost always reproduced because the model has a parameter for it; statistics the model does not fit directly (`"sd"` for over-dispersion, `"max"`/`"min"` for the tails, `"skew"`, `"n_zero"` for counts) are more informative. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#359adb6f .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_stat(stat="sd") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_stat(stat = "sd") ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_stat(stat = "sd") ``` ::: See [`m.diag.ppc_stat`](../reference/diag.qmd#ppc_stat) for further information regarding the list of arguments. ## Sensitivity ### Prior sensitivity Overlays the posteriors from models fitted with different priors to assess how much the conclusions change when the priors vary. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#94947f08 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Refit the same model with a tighter prior on b posteriors_weak = m.posteriors def model_strong(weight, height): a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name="a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 0.1, name="b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name="s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs=height, shape=(weight.shape[0],)) m.fit(model_strong, num_samples=500, num_chains=4) m.diag.prior_sensitivity([posteriors_weak, m.posteriors], labels=["weak prior", "strong prior"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## R ```r # Refit the same model with a tighter prior on b posteriors_weak <- m$posteriors model_strong <- function(weight, height) { a <- bf.dist.normal(178, 20, name = "a") b <- bf.dist.log_normal(0, 0.1, name = "b") s <- bf.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = "s") bf.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs = height) } m$fit(model_strong, num_samples = 500, num_chains = 4) m$diag$prior_sensitivity(list(posteriors_weak, m$posteriors), labels = list("weak prior", "strong prior")) ``` ## Julia ```julia # Refit the same model with a tighter prior on b posteriors_weak = m.posteriors @BF function model_strong(weight, height) a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name = "a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 0.1, name = "b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = "s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs = height) end m.fit(model_strong, num_samples = 500, num_chains = 4) @pyplot m.diag.prior_sensitivity([posteriors_weak, m.posteriors], labels = ["weak prior", "strong prior"]) ``` ::: #### Declaring the prior variations (parallel) Instead of refitting by hand, declare which priors vary. The model takes the bf instance `m` first, then the data, then the prior hyper-parameters (their defaults are the baseline). `prior_sensitivity` fits the baseline plus **one variation at a time** (each prior moved alone, the others at baseline) in parallel, through [`run_simulations`](Parallel%20simulations.qmd), and plots the results. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#869b5f6a .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} def model_decl(m, weight, height, a_sd=20.0, b_sd=1.0): a = m.dist.normal(178, a_sd, name="a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, b_sd, name="b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name="s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs=height, shape=(weight.shape[0],)) fig, table = m.diag.prior_sensitivity( model_decl, priors={"b_sd": [0.1, 0.5, 2.0], "a_sd": [5, 50]}, # 1 + 5 = 6 fits obs=dict(weight=m.df.weight.to_numpy(dtype="float32"), height=m.df.height.to_numpy(dtype="float32")), fit_kwargs=dict(num_samples=500, num_chains=1), progress=False, return_results=True) # table: mean, sd, HDI and shift_sd vs baseline fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` An NVIDIA GPU may be present on this machine, but a CUDA-enabled jaxlib is not installed. ``` ::: ::: ## R ```{.r .no-test} model <- function(m, weight, height, a_sd = 20, b_sd = 1) { a <- m$dist$normal(178, a_sd, name = "a") b <- m$dist$log_normal(0, b_sd, name = "b") s <- m$dist$uniform(0, 50, name = "s") m$dist$normal(a + b * weight, s, obs = height, name = "height") } out <- m$diag$prior_sensitivity( model, priors = list(b_sd = list(0.1, 0.5, 2.0), a_sd = list(5, 50)), # 1 + 5 = 6 fits obs = list(weight = weight, height = height), fit_kwargs = list(num_samples = 500L, num_chains = 1L), return_results = TRUE) # out[[1]]: figure, out[[2]]: table ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .no-test} @sim function model(m, weight, height; a_sd = 20.0, b_sd = 1.0) a = m.dist.normal(178, a_sd, name = "a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, b_sd, name = "b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = "s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs = height, name = "height") end fig, table = m.diag.prior_sensitivity( model, priors = Dict("b_sd" => [0.1, 0.5, 2.0], "a_sd" => [5, 50]), # 1 + 5 = 6 fits obs = Dict("weight" => weight, "height" => height), fit_kwargs = Dict("num_samples" => 500, "num_chains" => 1), return_results = true) ``` ::: The default plot (`plot="by_prior"`) has **one row per varied prior** and one column per parameter: each cell shows the baseline posterior (grey, dashed) and the posteriors when *that* prior alone is varied. `plot="shift"` gives a dot plot of the posterior-mean shift (in baseline sd) per variation, and `plot="overlay"` puts every fit in one panel per parameter. `mode="grid"` crosses all the lists instead (captures interactions, but the number of fits is the product of the list lengths); `joint={"all tighter": {"a_sd": 5, "b_sd": 0.1}}` adds scenarios where several priors move together. `shift_sd` is the change of the posterior mean from the baseline, in baseline posterior sd. Use them with caution. ### HMC diagnostics: divergences and energy ::: {#fe60a222 .cell execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} ::: {.callout-warning} ⚠️This function is still in development. Use it with caution. ⚠️ ::: ::: ::: Check this plot first: if the sampler failed, the other diagnostics are not meaningful. - **Top row, one panel per chain:** the distribution of the energy E around its mean (blue, *marginal energy*) and of its change between two successive iterations, ΔE (orange, *energy transition*). When the two histograms have about the same width, the sampler can cross the whole posterior from one iteration to the next. When ΔE is much narrower than E, it explores the tails badly (typical of a hierarchical "funnel"). The panel title gives E-BFMI = Σ ΔE² / Σ (E − Ē)²; values below 0.3 are flagged with ⚠. - **Bottom row:** the number of divergent transitions per chain (ideal: 0). A divergence means that the integrator failed in a region of strong curvature, which is then under-explored. With a few divergences, raise `target_accept` (0.95–0.99); with many, reparametrise (for example a non-centred random effect). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#a3436db1 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.divergence_energy() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
